title: Writing Maintainable Workflow Steps knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Writing Maintainable Workflow Steps?
options: Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Maintainable steps are small, named for their intent, fail clearly, and avoid unnecessary shell complexity or repeated inline logic.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
questions.answer_key: Maintainable steps are small, named for their intent, fail clearly, and avoid unnecessary shell complexity or repeated inline logic.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of writing maintainable workflow steps: Maintainable steps are small, named for their intent, fail clearly, and avoid unnecessary shell complexity or repeated inline logic. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.prompt: A team is working with “Clear step naming”. Which practice best fits this topic?
options: Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.
questions.answer_key: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.
questions.explanation: Clear step naming: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action. Apply the guidance to the actual event, runner, permissions, or artifact boundary and test the relevant case.

questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to writing maintainable workflow steps?
options: Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: Maintainable steps are small, named for their intent, fail clearly, and avoid unnecessary shell complexity or repeated inline logic. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
